6901.sentence: The playbook includes 10 principles civil servants should uphold when using AI.
6901.sourceTitle: AI Playbook for the UK Government
6901.body: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology

6909.sentence: As technology evolves, so too will our approach, ensuring we remain at the forefront of responsible innovation - always guided by the principle that technology must serve people.
6909.sourceTitle: AI Playbook for the UK Government
6909.body: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology

6912.sentence: You should learn about AI technology to understand what it can and cannot do, and the potential risks it poses.
6912.sourceTitle: AI Playbook for the UK Government
6912.body: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
6912.headingPath: Principle 1: You know what AI is and what its limitations are

6912.sentence: You should understand how to use AI tools safely and responsibly, employ techniques to increase the accuracy and correctness of their outputs, and have a process in place to test them.
6912.sourceTitle: AI Playbook for the UK Government
6912.body: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
6912.headingPath: Principle 1: You know what AI is and what its limitations are

6913.sentence: Your use of AI tools must be lawful and responsible.
6913.sourceTitle: AI Playbook for the UK Government
6913.body: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
6913.headingPath: Principle 2: You use AI lawfully, ethically and responsibly

6913.sentence: You must ensure that AI systems generate a positive impact on stakeholders and civil society at large while minimising potential harms as much as possible.
6913.sourceTitle: AI Playbook for the UK Government
6913.body: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
6913.headingPath: Principle 2: You use AI lawfully, ethically and responsibly

6913.sentence: When defining and deploying AI systems, you must understand people’s needs and priorities by conducting user research and engaging with the public as appropriate, including civil society groups, underrepresented individuals, those most likely to experience harm, NGOs, academia and industry.
6913.sourceTitle: AI Playbook for the UK Government
6913.body: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
6913.headingPath: Principle 2: You use AI lawfully, ethically and responsibly

6913.sentence: You should seek legal advice on the development and use of AI and engage with compliance, legal and data protection experts in your organisation early in your journey, including during product development.
6913.sourceTitle: AI Playbook for the UK Government
6913.body: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
6913.headingPath: Principle 2: You use AI lawfully, ethically and responsibly

6913.sentence: You should seek data protection advice on your use of AI.
6913.sourceTitle: AI Playbook for the UK Government
6913.body: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
6913.headingPath: Principle 2: You use AI lawfully, ethically and responsibly

6913.sentence: You should establish and communicate how you will address ethical concerns throughout your project, from design to deployment, so that diverse and inclusive participation is built into the project life cycle.
6913.sourceTitle: AI Playbook for the UK Government
6913.body: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
6913.headingPath: Principle 2: You use AI lawfully, ethically and responsibly

6913.sentence: You should also consider the ethical principles presented in this playbook, and establish robust measures to suit your technological and deployment context.
6913.sourceTitle: AI Playbook for the UK Government
6913.body: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
6913.headingPath: Principle 2: You use AI lawfully, ethically and responsibly

6913.sentence: You should consider all potential sources of bias throughout the development life cycle, including unrepresentative data sets and deployment scenarios that have unfair or undesirable impacts.
6913.sourceTitle: AI Playbook for the UK Government
6913.body: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
6913.headingPath: Principle 2: You use AI lawfully, ethically and responsibly

6913.sentence: You should understand and manage the environmental impact of the AI systems you are planning to use.
6913.sourceTitle: AI Playbook for the UK Government
6913.body: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
6913.headingPath: Principle 2: You use AI lawfully, ethically and responsibly

6913.sentence: You should also use AI technologies only when relevant, appropriate and proportionate.
6913.sourceTitle: AI Playbook for the UK Government
6913.body: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
6913.headingPath: Principle 2: You use AI lawfully, ethically and responsibly

6914.sentence: When building and deploying AI services, you must make sure that they are secure to use and resilient to cyber attacks, as laid out in the Government Cyber Security Strategy.
6914.sourceTitle: AI Playbook for the UK Government
6914.body: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
6914.headingPath: Principle 3: You know how to use AI securely

6914.sentence: Your service must comply with the Secure by Design principles, which were developed by the Central Digital and Data Office (CDDO), and the government’s Cyber Security Standard.
6914.sourceTitle: AI Playbook for the UK Government
6914.body: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
6914.headingPath: Principle 3: You know how to use AI securely

6917.sentence: You should be open to solutions involving AI because they can allow organisations to develop new or faster approaches to the delivery of public services, can provide a springboard for more creative and innovative thinking about policy and public sector problems, and help your team with time-consuming tasks.

6917.sentence: However, you should also be open to the conclusion that, sometimes, AI is not the best solution for your problem: it may be more easily solved with more established technologies.

7331.headingPath: 3. Evaluation methods > 3.6 Value for money evaluation methods

7967.sentence: Practitioners should monetise social costs and social benefits where possible, to provide a common pound sterling estimate of social value.
Practitioners should look beyond impacts on the originating organisation.
They should also consider significant costs, benefits and risks for other public bodies, businesses, households and charities.
Even if a proposal is focused on a single geographical area, practitioners should consider whether the proposal might have significant impacts elsewhere.
Social costs and social benefits should be calculated over the lifetime of the proposal, from initial construction or development, through to termination or decommissioning.
Practitioners should adjust their estimates of monetisable social costs and social benefits to remove the effect of general price inflation.
Monetisable costs and benefits should also be discounted using the Social Time Preference Rate (STPR).
Practitioners should consider the risks and uncertainties around different options.

They should assess the chances of different degrees of success or failure in achieving the proposal’s objectives, and the possibility that costs, benefits and distributional impacts will differ from those anticipated in appraisal.
Practitioners should include risk costs in appraisal.
Practitioners should pay particular attention to fraud risk where public money is distributed through grants, loans or other payments.
Practitioners should explicitly adjust their appraisals for optimism bias.
Practitioners should account for optimism bias by increasing their estimates of social costs and project durations, and decreasing their estimates of social benefits.
Practitioners should conduct sensitivity analysis to examine how changes in key assumptions, like costs, might affect the summary metrics of the appraisal.
Practitioners should also calculate switching values.
Practitioners should assess how different groups or places are affected by a proposal.
In particular, distributional analysis should be used to illustrate the effects of a proposal on those groups with the protected characteristics defined in the Equality Act 2010.

10722.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.4 Define the scope and break it down into components

10722.sentence: The structure should be retained and stored appropriately, both for review purposes and for potential future use in planning and managing similar work, thus saving significant cost and effort.
10722.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10722.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.4 Define the scope and break it down into components

10723.sentence: The organisation of work activities should be determined by the needs of the work and the associated constraints, and can be managed in different ways.
10723.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10723.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.5 Decide and sequence work activities

10724.sentence: A schedule should be shown in terms of public sector planning timescales, showing activities within or across financial years, usually broken down into shorter periods (quarters, months, weeks or days), depending on the work and granularity of planning.
10724.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10724.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.6 Develop the plan

10724.sentence: At this point, however, timescales should be given as ranges rather than point estimates.
10724.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10724.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.6 Develop the plan

10724.sentence: As the schedule develops, probabilistic analysis should also be conducted, for example Monte Carlo or curve analysis, in order to test and refine the schedule.
10724.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10724.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.6 Develop the plan

10724.sentence: By the time a plan is ready to be approved, the overall schedule should be robust and evidence-based.
10724.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10724.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.6 Develop the plan

10724.sentence: The plan should include critical milestones and, where appropriate, the critical path, critical chain, time-boxing or sprints proposed for delivery.
10724.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10724.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.6 Develop the plan

10724.sentence: It should also make appropriate provision for risk and contingency, and align fully to cost and resource plans.
10724.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10724.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.6 Develop the plan

10724.sentence: More detailed activity schedules may be developed within each work package to manage and control delivery, but these should always be traceable back to, and within the tolerances agreed for, the approved and baselined schedule.
10724.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10724.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.6 Develop the plan

10724.sentence: The people capability and other resources required to carry out the work should be identified.
10724.actor: other resources required to carry out the work
10724.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10724.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.6 Develop the plan

10724.sentence: Capability requirements should be estimated for each work activity, both in terms of competency (professional skills, both type and level) and capacity (how many people are needed).
10724.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10724.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.6 Develop the plan

10724.sentence: Resource planning should develop progressively, moving from initial estimates to granular planning linked to each work activity within the schedule.
10724.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10724.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.6 Develop the plan

10724.sentence: Planning should also consider how resources can be balanced and optimised across work activities (sometimes known as resource levelling), to avoid peaks and gaps in activities which mean people or other resources are over-stretched or under-used at different points through the life cycle.
10724.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10724.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.6 Develop the plan

10724.sentence: Planning should also identify when activities are completed and resources are no longer needed, so that they can be reallocated or moved on in an appropriate and considerate way.
10724.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10724.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.6 Develop the plan

10724.sentence: Resource requirements can be estimated in hours or days, but should be set out on a full time equivalent (FTE) basis, in work days aligned to the schedule, with costs per FTE identified so that they can be costed accordingly.
10724.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10724.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.6 Develop the plan

10724.sentence: When ready for approval, the integrated plan should include a robust, evidence-based resource plan, fully aligned to the schedule (sometimes referred to as a resource-loaded schedule), and making provision for risk and contingency.
10724.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10724.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.6 Develop the plan

10724.sentence: The total benefits arising from the work should be identified by work component, showing when they arise across the life cycle (including those arising during delivery).
10724.actor: total benefits arising from the work
10724.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10724.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.6 Develop the plan

10724.sentence: The total costs for the work should be determined, broken down by work component, and allocated across the schedule to show when funding is needed.
10724.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10724.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.6 Develop the plan

10724.sentence: Both benefits and costs should be presented by financial year, broken down as appropriate, and identified in terms of public sector expenditure funding categories and types of social cost and benefit.
10724.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10724.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.6 Develop the plan

10724.sentence: As for other planning, estimation of benefits and costs is progressive as planning becomes more detailed, and the estimates at the time of approval should be based on robust, evidence-based estimates, fully aligned to the schedule, and factoring in risk, contingency and optimism bias in line with requirements set out in the Green Book (requires sign in), Cost estimating guidance (requires sign in) and Best practice in benchmarking (see also Chapter 19: Benefits management and Chapter 29: Finance).
10724.actor: estimates at the time of approval
10724.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10724.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.6 Develop the plan

10724.sentence: These should follow the same principles as for other elements of planning, be fully aligned to the schedule and integrated with other planning elements as part of the overall plan ready for approval and baselining.
10724.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10724.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.6 Develop the plan

10725.sentence: All elements of the plan, particularly the work breakdown structure, schedule, resource, cost and benefits plans, should be brought together and reviewed to ensure:
10725.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10725.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.7 Integrate and review the plan

10726.sentence: Once the plan has been found acceptable to the reviewers, it should be submitted for approval to the appropriate higher-level decision makers.
10726.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10726.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.8 Approve, baseline and maintain the plan

10726.sentence: If the plan does not appear sufficiently robust or viable to enable delivery of the business case, it should be reconsidered and either changes made to make it viable or a decision taken not to proceed.
10726.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10726.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.8 Approve, baseline and maintain the plan

10726.sentence: This should include supply chain plans where relevant.
10726.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10726.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.8 Approve, baseline and maintain the plan

10726.sentence: Progress against the plan should be monitored and controlled (see Chapter 17: Controlling) and reported (see Chapter 18: Reporting).
10726.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10726.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.8 Approve, baseline and maintain the plan

10726.sentence: Plans should be reviewed and updated, taking account of progress and any changes in assumptions or estimates, especially before significant decision points, such as gates.
10726.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10726.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.8 Approve, baseline and maintain the plan

10727.sentence: Once the programme or project has been completed, the planning framework should be closed and information archived in accordance with the sponsoring organisation’s information retention policy.
10727.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10727.headingPath: Chapter 16: Planning > 16.6 How to plan > 16.6.3 Key planning activities > 16.6.3.9 Close the planning framework

10731.sentence: Managing public money (requires sign in) states that ‘acting within the authority of the minister(s) to whom they are responsible, the accounting officer shall ensure that the organisation, and any arm’s length bodies it sponsors, operates effectively and to a high standard of probity’.
10731.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10731.headingPath: Chapter 17: Controlling > 17.3 Why control the work?

10732.sentence: Control should also be forward-looking, with the aim of prompting action to keep the work on course to meet the defined objectives, addressing issues, taking advantage of opportunities and reducing the impact of threats, whilst verifying what has already happened.
10732.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government

10732.sentence: The frequency of the cycle should be both informal, with managers reacting to day-to-day circumstances, and also formal, for example synchronised with the reporting cycle.
10732.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government

10732.sentence: The further up the project delivery hierarchy, the more holistic and wide ranging the analysis should be.
10732.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government

10733.sentence: Each level of the project delivery hierarchy should be controlled by its controlling manager: for example, a project manager controls a project.
10733.actor: level of the project delivery hierarchy
10733.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10733.headingPath: Chapter 17: Controlling > 17.5 Who controls the work?

10737.sentence: Progress information should not only be looked at solely in relation to its ‘date’ but also in relation to trends, including in the supply chain.
10737.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10737.headingPath: Chapter 17: Controlling > 17.6 How to control the work > 17.6.1 What to consider when controlling the work > 17.6.1.4 Recognising instability

10741.sentence: This should match the nature, scale and complexity of the portfolio, programme or project, and the expected delivery approach.
10741.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10741.headingPath: Chapter 17: Controlling > 17.6 How to control the work > 17.6.2 Preparing to control the work > 17.6.2.1 Define the control framework

10741.sentence: Controlling in government should also take account of central government and organisational requirements, particularly in relation to spending reviews, annual business planning, and department-specific HM Treasury delegated limits, and with the wider approach to functional controls set out in the department’s memorandum of understanding with HM Treasury.
10741.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10741.headingPath: Chapter 17: Controlling > 17.6 How to control the work > 17.6.2 Preparing to control the work > 17.6.2.1 Define the control framework

10742.sentence: The control information should result directly from doing the work wherever possible, as this improves accuracy and reduces additional work for the team.
10742.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10742.headingPath: Chapter 17: Controlling > 17.6 How to control the work > 17.6.2 Preparing to control the work > 17.6.2.2 Determine what needs to be controlled

10744.sentence: The units should relate directly to the work where possible.
10744.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10744.headingPath: Chapter 17: Controlling > 17.6 How to control the work > 17.6.2 Preparing to control the work > 17.6.2.4 Decide what measurement units to use

10744.sentence: Tracking measures should be the same as used for planning to ensure they are comparable.
10744.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10744.headingPath: Chapter 17: Controlling > 17.6 How to control the work > 17.6.2 Preparing to control the work > 17.6.2.4 Decide what measurement units to use

10748.sentence: The approach to controlling the work should be defined including any processes, methods, tools and techniques to be used.
10748.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10748.headingPath: Chapter 17: Controlling > 17.6 How to control the work > 17.6.3 Key activities in controlling the work > 17.6.3.2 Develop and maintain the control framework

10748.sentence: The framework should be maintained to address relevant feedback from its use.
10748.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10748.headingPath: Chapter 17: Controlling > 17.6 How to control the work > 17.6.3 Key activities in controlling the work > 17.6.3.2 Develop and maintain the control framework

10749.sentence: The higher-level controlling manager should ensure they are receiving the information they need, whether informally, as reports or by drawing them off management information systems when needed.
10749.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10749.headingPath: Chapter 17: Controlling > 17.6 How to control the work > 17.6.3 Key activities in controlling the work > 17.6.3.3 Oversee controlling

10749.sentence: They are likely to be dealing with information relating to a large number of work components and should make sure that the information is consistent and usable.
10749.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10749.headingPath: Chapter 17: Controlling > 17.6 How to control the work > 17.6.3 Key activities in controlling the work > 17.6.3.3 Oversee controlling

10749.sentence: They should look for overall trends both with individual work components but also across work components,
10749.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10749.headingPath: Chapter 17: Controlling > 17.6 How to control the work > 17.6.3 Key activities in controlling the work > 17.6.3.3 Oversee controlling

10750.sentence: Work should be undertaken in accordance with the plans and using the delivery approaches and controls defined in the governance and management framework.
10750.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10750.headingPath: Chapter 17: Controlling > 17.6 How to control the work > 17.6.3 Key activities in controlling the work > 17.6.3.4 Do the work

10751.sentence: The progress of the work should be tracked using the measures and frequencies prescribed in the control framework, ensuring that the information is timely and reflects observable progress where physically apparent.
10751.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10751.headingPath: Chapter 17: Controlling > 17.6 How to control the work > 17.6.3 Key activities in controlling the work > 17.6.3.5 Track progress

10751.sentence: Information should be drawn on from each relevant Part E: Planning and control and Part F: Solution delivery practice and verified to ensure it is sufficient for a reliable view to be taken regarding the current status of the work.
10751.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10751.headingPath: Chapter 17: Controlling > 17.6 How to control the work > 17.6.3 Key activities in controlling the work > 17.6.3.5 Track progress

10752.sentence: The status of the work should be assessed and analysed, using the defined approaches.
10752.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10752.headingPath: Chapter 17: Controlling > 17.6 How to control the work > 17.6.3 Key activities in controlling the work > 17.6.3.6 Assess and analyse status

10752.sentence: Material variances and deviations, and inconsistencies in information should be noted together with understanding the reasons for them, for example using root cause analysis techniques.
10752.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10752.headingPath: Chapter 17: Controlling > 17.6 How to control the work > 17.6.3 Key activities in controlling the work > 17.6.3.6 Assess and analyse status

10754.sentence: Once the control framework is no longer needed it should be closed.
10754.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10754.headingPath: Chapter 17: Controlling > 17.6 How to control the work > 17.6.3 Key activities in controlling the work > 17.6.3.8 Close the control framework

10757.sentence: Reports should be timely, realistic and meet the needs of the recipients.
10757.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government

10759.sentence: A report should be derived from the analysis and insight gained from controlling the work.
10759.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government

10759.sentence: Reporting should not replace direct conversations, meetings and other interactions needed to manage teams and control the work.
10759.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government

10759.sentence: Work should be undertaken in accordance with the plan using the delivery approaches defined in the governance and management framework, with progress tracked using appropriate measures.
10759.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government

10759.sentence: Action should then be taken to address any variances or problems.
10759.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government

10759.sentence: For this reason, reporting should be forward- looking.
10759.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government

10759.sentence: Reports should meet the needs of those receiving them.
10759.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government

10759.sentence: Each report format should be designed with the recipients in mind.
10759.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government

10759.sentence: The higher up the hierarchy, the more outcome- and benefit-focused, holistic and wide ranging the reporting should be.
10759.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government

10759.sentence: The frequency of the active reporting cycle should be both informal with managers reacting to day-to-day circumstances and also formal, usually with defined time periods, usually synchronised with the control cycle and often feeding into wider organisational reporting.
10759.actor: frequency of the active reporting cycle
10759.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government

10761.sentence: A work package manager should report on their work to the respective project manager or manager of other work.
10761.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10761.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.5 Who reports to whom? > 18.5.2 Upward reporting

10766.sentence: The reporting manager should agree, as part of defining the report, how the recipient would prefer specific requests highlighted.
10766.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10766.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.1 What to consider when reporting on the work > 18.6.1.2 Highlighting the important information and action needed

10768.sentence: Information provided by a work package manager should be gathered with that from other work packages and collated at project level by the project manager.
10768.actor: Information provided by a work package manager
10768.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10768.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.2 Preparing for reporting > 18.6.2.1 Understand who needs a report and why

10769.sentence: Having understood who needs a report and why, a reporting framework should be defined which can provide the information recipients need, when they need it.
10769.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10769.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.2 Preparing for reporting > 18.6.2.2 Define the reporting framework

10769.sentence: The reporting framework should define who reviews and approves a report:
10769.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10769.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.2 Preparing for reporting > 18.6.2.2 Define the reporting framework

10769.sentence: when a report is drafted on behalf of the reporting manager, the reporting manager should agree with the author how and when the report needs to be approved by them
10769.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10769.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.2 Preparing for reporting > 18.6.2.2 Define the reporting framework

10769.sentence: Having a report reviewed by multiple parties should be avoided if possible as this adds delays.
10769.actor: Having a report reviewed by multiple parties
10769.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10769.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.2 Preparing for reporting > 18.6.2.2 Define the reporting framework

10769.sentence: It should be noted, though, that some reports require a fuller review, for example where important or sensitive decisions depend on the information, or where it is to be published.
10769.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10769.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.2 Preparing for reporting > 18.6.2.2 Define the reporting framework

10770.sentence: A report should be timely, factual and realistic, highlighting where the work is heading and confirming progress to date.
10770.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10770.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.2 Preparing for reporting > 18.6.2.3 Determine the content of each report

10770.sentence: In every instance, recipients should consider why they need the information, and the reporting manager or author should consider why they are providing it.
10770.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10770.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.2 Preparing for reporting > 18.6.2.3 Determine the content of each report

10770.sentence: Each report should state the period or date the information relates to and the date on which the report was produced, or if drawn on-demand, the date it was created with date stamps for the constituent data.
10770.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10770.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.2 Preparing for reporting > 18.6.2.3 Determine the content of each report

10770.sentence: The form of a report should be appropriate and proportionate to the work being reported on and the roles being reported to.
10770.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10770.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.2 Preparing for reporting > 18.6.2.3 Determine the content of each report

10770.sentence: The rules for triggering exception reports should be defined, based on margins (tolerances) applied to the particular constraint being reported on.
10770.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10770.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.2 Preparing for reporting > 18.6.2.3 Determine the content of each report

10770.sentence: An exception report should contain a statement of the actual or forecast exception, a description of the planned recovery action and an estimate of the threat to the work plan in terms of benefits, schedule, cost and risk.
10770.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10770.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.2 Preparing for reporting > 18.6.2.3 Determine the content of each report

10770.sentence: Reporting for a programme, project, phase or work package should be tailored to the level of the report.
10770.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10770.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.2 Preparing for reporting > 18.6.2.3 Determine the content of each report

10770.sentence: Data should normally cover the current month, current financial year and life of the work.
10770.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10770.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.2 Preparing for reporting > 18.6.2.3 Determine the content of each report

10770.sentence: A typical programme or project level report should cover at least the following.
10770.actor: typical programme or project level report
10770.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10770.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.2 Preparing for reporting > 18.6.2.3 Determine the content of each report

10770.sentence: This should be consistent with the progress of deliverables and is typically shown in graphical form.
10770.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10770.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.2 Preparing for reporting > 18.6.2.3 Determine the content of each report

10770.sentence: Any forecast start or finish dates that are later than the planned should be shown separately, as slippage may affect the completion date (see 17.6.1.6 on choosing methods to assess and analyse the status of the work).
10770.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10770.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.2 Preparing for reporting > 18.6.2.3 Determine the content of each report

10770.sentence: These should be shown by category of expenditure and should identify any cash releasing benefit impacting on the financial baseline where relevant (see 29.6.3.7 on reporting on financial status).
10770.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10770.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.2 Preparing for reporting > 18.6.2.3 Determine the content of each report

10770.sentence: This should identify internal and external resources by category, and any current or forecast vacancies (see 28.6.1.4 on ensuring accurate resource monitoring).
10770.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10770.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.2 Preparing for reporting > 18.6.2.3 Determine the content of each report

10770.sentence: This should include any changes in the status of identified threats together with any newly identified threats, opportunities or issues.
10770.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10770.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.2 Preparing for reporting > 18.6.2.3 Determine the content of each report

10770.sentence: This might include testing data, user feedback or other measures of quality agreed for the solution, and should identify any concerns and action needed to address them (see 30.6 on how to manage quality).
10770.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10770.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.2 Preparing for reporting > 18.6.2.3 Determine the content of each report

10770.sentence: These should be shown by the relevant category of benefit; cash-releasing benefits can be included (see costs above) but care should be taken to highlight where these are also included as cash costs in financial reporting, to avoid double-counting (see 19.6.2.1 on understanding the objectives and desired outcomes).
10770.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10770.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.2 Preparing for reporting > 18.6.2.3 Determine the content of each report

10774.sentence: The governance and management framework should define what reports are needed and at what frequency to meet the needs of the recipients, contractual obligations (if any) and the level of information necessary to control the work at each level in the project delivery hierarchy.
10774.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10774.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.3 Key reporting activities > 18.6.3.2 Develop and maintain the reporting framework

10774.sentence: The framework should be maintained to address relevant feedback from its use.
10774.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10774.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.3 Key reporting activities > 18.6.3.2 Develop and maintain the reporting framework

10774.sentence: The reporting approach and methods should be planned and documented early in the life cycle of the work.
10774.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10774.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.3 Key reporting activities > 18.6.3.2 Develop and maintain the reporting framework

10774.sentence: Reporting needs should be defined, including but not limited to the content, author, recipients, frequency, confidentiality and format of each report needed.
10774.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10774.headingPath: Chapter 18: Reporting > 18.6 How to report on the work > 18.6.3 Key reporting activities > 18.6.3.2 Develop and maintain the reporting framework

10775.sentence: Those accountable at each level in the project delivery hierarchy should ensure they are receiving the information they need, either as reports or by drawing it from the data repositories.

10786.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.5 Who manages benefits?

10786.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.5 Who manages benefits?

10787.sentence: It should be possible to trace from any objective down to the benefits that deliver it, and from any benefit back up to the objective it supports, known as two-way traceability .

10787.sentence: Where policy proposals have been developed using a specific theory of change (see Chapter 2: Policy and evaluation), this should provide the initial basis for considering objectives and outcomes, and how these might map to benefits.

10787.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.1 What to consider when managing benefits > 19.6.1.1 Linking benefits to objectives and outcomes

10787.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.1 What to consider when managing benefits > 19.6.1.1 Linking benefits to objectives and outcomes

10788.sentence: Starting from the proposed objectives and outcomes, and exploring what these mean in practice with different groups of stakeholders, should help identify the primary benefits to be included in planning and investment appraisal.

10789.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.1 What to consider when managing benefits > 19.6.1.3 Assessing and prioritising benefits

10789.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.1 What to consider when managing benefits > 19.6.1.3 Assessing and prioritising benefits

10789.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.1 What to consider when managing benefits > 19.6.1.3 Assessing and prioritising benefits

10790.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.1 What to consider when managing benefits > 19.6.1.4 Setting the time horizon for benefits realisation

10791.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.1 What to consider when managing benefits > 19.6.1.5 Controlling changes to benefits assumptions

10792.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.1 What to consider when managing benefits > 19.6.1.6 Linking benefits management and evaluation

10793.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.2 Preparing to manage benefits > 19.6.2.1 Understand the aims of the work

10794.sentence: The framework should be tailored to the nature, scale and complexity of the work, and should be compatible with any relevant frameworks at organisation, portfolio or programme level, and with requirements in the Green Book (requires sign in) on benefits in business case development and investment appraisal.

10797.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.3 Key activities in managing benefits > 19.6.3.3 Develop and maintain the benefits management framework

10797.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.3 Key activities in managing benefits > 19.6.3.3 Develop and maintain the benefits management framework

10798.sentence: The benefits manager should ensure that benefits management is carried out in accordance with the benefits management framework and fulfils its purpose.
10798.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10798.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.3 Key activities in managing benefits > 19.6.3.4 Oversee benefits management

10798.sentence: The benefits management framework should be kept under review, taking account of any changes in the context and nature of the work, to ensure that it remains effective through the life cycle or (in the case of a portfolio) in preparing for the next planning cycle.

10798.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.3 Key activities in managing benefits > 19.6.3.4 Oversee benefits management

10799.sentence: Benefits should be identified as early as possible, ideally starting as part of initial policy formulation, and considered further during work on feasibility.

10799.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.3 Key activities in managing benefits > 19.6.3.5 Identify and categorise a benefit

10799.sentence: Identification should start from the objectives, drivers and outcomes for the work, and what this might look like in terms of critical success factor s and potential benefits.

10799.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.3 Key activities in managing benefits > 19.6.3.5 Identify and categorise a benefit

10799.sentence: Wherever possible, benefits should be described at a level of detail where they can be managed effectively and assigned to a single owner.

10799.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.3 Key activities in managing benefits > 19.6.3.5 Identify and categorise a benefit

10799.sentence: For business case purposes, this should follow the classifications in the Green Book (requires sign in) for example as monetisable and cash-releasing or not, or as non-monetisable, either quantitative or qualitative.

10799.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.3 Key activities in managing benefits > 19.6.3.5 Identify and categorise a benefit

10799.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.3 Key activities in managing benefits > 19.6.3.5 Identify and categorise a benefit

10799.sentence: Other information can be added progressively to the benefits register, which should be kept updated as decisions on solution options are taken, benefits targets are set and benefits ownership assigned.

10799.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.3 Key activities in managing benefits > 19.6.3.5 Identify and categorise a benefit

10800.sentence: A forecast should be developed with, and agreed by, each benefits owner, with measures, baselines, targets and timescales, assumptions, dependencies and risks documented alongside, creating a benefit profile for each benefit.
10800.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10800.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.3 Key activities in managing benefits > 19.6.3.6 Value and appraise a benefit

10800.sentence: For annual planning cycles, benefits appraisal should be tailored to organisational objectives, for example to prioritise certain categories or classes of benefit within the portfolio.

10800.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.3 Key activities in managing benefits > 19.6.3.6 Value and appraise a benefit

10800.sentence: As such, it forms an important part of the economic case in the outline business case or programme business case, and should be closely integrated with wider planning and business case development.

10800.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.3 Key activities in managing benefits > 19.6.3.6 Value and appraise a benefit

10800.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.3 Key activities in managing benefits > 19.6.3.6 Value and appraise a benefit

10800.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.3 Key activities in managing benefits > 19.6.3.6 Value and appraise a benefit

10800.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.3 Key activities in managing benefits > 19.6.3.6 Value and appraise a benefit

10800.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.3 Key activities in managing benefits > 19.6.3.6 Value and appraise a benefit

10800.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.3 Key activities in managing benefits > 19.6.3.6 Value and appraise a benefit

10802.headingPath: Chapter 19: Benefits management > 19.6 How to manage benefits? > 19.6.3 Key activities in managing benefits > 19.6.3.8 Realise the benefit

10802.sentence: Progress on realising each benefit should be monitored and reported against agreed metrics at agreed frequency, depending on the nature of the benefit, how quickly it accrues and how easy it is to measure.

10849.sentence: In the case of a major issue which cannot be resolved, the issue should be escalated to the appropriate level for a decision on possible termination of the work.
10849.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10849.headingPath: Chapter 21: Issue management > 21.6.3 Key activities in managing issue management > 21.6.3.6 Respond to the issue

10849.sentence: The response actions should be proportionate to the impact and be value for money.
10849.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10849.headingPath: Chapter 21: Issue management > 21.6.3 Key activities in managing issue management > 21.6.3.6 Respond to the issue

10849.sentence: The issue owner should assign actions to one or more named individuals, known as the action owner(s) to undertake this work.
10849.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10849.headingPath: Chapter 21: Issue management > 21.6.3 Key activities in managing issue management > 21.6.3.6 Respond to the issue

10850.sentence: The actions taken in response to the issue should be monitored to check they are effective.
10850.actor: actions taken in response to the issue
10850.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10850.headingPath: Chapter 21: Issue management > 21.6.3 Key activities in managing issue management > 21.6.3.7 Monitor and report the issue

10850.sentence: Those who need to know about the issue should be kept informed.
10850.actor: Those who need to know about the issue
10850.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10850.headingPath: Chapter 21: Issue management > 21.6.3 Key activities in managing issue management > 21.6.3.7 Monitor and report the issue

10850.sentence: The issues register is a primary source of management information used in reporting (see Chapter 18: Reporting) and should be updated on an ongoing basis to reflect the current understanding of the issue, its impact and the response actions.
10850.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10850.headingPath: Chapter 21: Issue management > 21.6.3 Key activities in managing issue management > 21.6.3.7 Monitor and report the issue

10851.sentence: An issue should be closed once it no longer needs monitoring and the response actions have been completed.
10851.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10851.headingPath: Chapter 21: Issue management > 21.6.3 Key activities in managing issue management > 21.6.3.8 Close the issue

10851.sentence: There should be an agreed procedure for closing issues, for example seeking approval from the appropriate decision-making body in the team, as determined in the governance and management framework.
10851.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10851.headingPath: Chapter 21: Issue management > 21.6.3 Key activities in managing issue management > 21.6.3.8 Close the issue

10851.sentence: Closed issues should be kept on the register, stating when and why they were closed and by whom as this information is important for managing aggregated issues, identifying likely sources of risks (see Chapter 20: Risk management), for maintaining traceability (see Chapter 23: Traceability management), and when conducting lessons learned reviews (see Chapter 38: Learning from experience ).
10851.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10851.headingPath: Chapter 21: Issue management > 21.6.3 Key activities in managing issue management > 21.6.3.8 Close the issue

10852.sentence: Once the work has been completed and issue management is no longer needed, the management framework should be merged into the management framework for the solution or closed, retaining information and data in accordance with the delivery and sponsoring body’s information retention policy.
10852.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10852.headingPath: Chapter 21: Issue management > 21.6.3 Key activities in managing issue management > 21.6.3.9 Close the issue management framework

10855.sentence: Changes are inevitable in project delivery but they should only be implemented through a structured change control process that protects the baseline against scope creep.
10855.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government

10855.sentence: Identify which aspects of the work should be subject to change control.
10855.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government

10855.sentence: Every change request should be assessed through an impact assessment and only necessary and beneficial changes which further the objectives of the work should be approved.
10855.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government

10857.sentence: Where a change exceeds tolerance, but is considered necessary or beneficial, the change request should be escalated to the appropriate level.
10857.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10857.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.4 What is change control?

10858.sentence: Accountability and responsibility for change control should be clearly defined within the governance and management framework and reviewed on a regular basis, to avoid duplication or gaps.
10858.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10858.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.5 Who controls changes?

10858.sentence: If a dedicated change control manager is not necessary, the portfolio, programme or project manager, as appropriate, should undertake the role.
10858.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10858.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.5 Who controls changes?

10858.sentence: To keep change control effective, care should be taken to not allocate too many changes to one owner.
10858.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10858.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.5 Who controls changes?

candidateConflicts.sourceTitle: The Digital, Data and Technology Playbook
candidateConflicts.sentence: Care should be taken where any IP will be used in different jurisdictions as there may well be different rules regarding registration or even whether it needs to be registered at all.

10859.sentence: Decisions on change requests should be made by those who have the authority to do so, within their assigned tolerances and who own the affected configuration items.
10859.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10859.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.1 What to consider when controlling change > 22.6.1.1 Identifying the right decision-makers at the right level

10859.sentence: If the change impacts another portfolio, programme or project, the decision maker should have accountability for balancing the competing needs of the work.
10859.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10859.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.1 What to consider when controlling change > 22.6.1.1 Identifying the right decision-makers at the right level

10859.sentence: To ensure effective decision-making a tiered system of delegation should be defined and established in the change control framework (see 22.6.3.2 on developing the change control framework).
10859.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10859.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.1 What to consider when controlling change > 22.6.1.1 Identifying the right decision-makers at the right level

10859.sentence: Portfolio, programme and project managers should have permissible tolerances within which they can approve changes without escalation.
10859.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10859.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.1 What to consider when controlling change > 22.6.1.1 Identifying the right decision-makers at the right level

10860.sentence: Enough information should be recorded to enable decisions to be made and action taken.
10860.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10860.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.1 What to consider when controlling change > 22.6.1.2 Assessing changes to an appropriate level of detail

10862.sentence: The record of changes should be open to the core team so they are aware of what is proposed, and can take a view on whether their work could be affected.
10862.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10862.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.1 What to consider when controlling change > 22.6.1.4 Being open and collaborative

10864.sentence: This informs the choice about which aspects of the work should be subject to change control and who should have authority for decisions.
10864.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10864.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.2 Preparing to control changes > 22.6.2.2 Understand the nature and context of the work

10867.sentence: The approach to change control should be defined including any processes, methods, tools and techniques to be used.
10867.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10867.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.2 Develop and maintain the change control framework

10867.sentence: The framework should be maintained to address relevant feedback from its use.
10867.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10867.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.2 Develop and maintain the change control framework

10868.sentence: Therefore, the change control framework should be under continuous review to ensure it remains effective.
10868.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10868.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.3 Oversee change control

10869.sentence: Once put forward, the change request should be registered and an owner assigned by the change control manager.
10869.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10869.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.4 Identify a change

10870.sentence: The change request should be assessed and validated to understand its impact on baselines for the plan, solution design and the management documentation, interdependent work and whether it is necessary or desirable.
10870.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10870.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.5 Assess and plan the change

10870.sentence: The change request should be classified in accordance with the pre-defined categorisations in the control framework.
10870.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10870.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.5 Assess and plan the change

10870.sentence: There are different techniques that can be used to evaluate the possible options (which should include doing nothing) and their impacts.
10870.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10870.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.5 Assess and plan the change

10870.sentence: The proposed change should be planned in draft (see Chapter 16: Planning), with an understanding of how to incorporate it into the wider work and implement it.
10870.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10870.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.5 Assess and plan the change

10870.sentence: Residual risks should be recorded and addressed.
10870.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10870.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.5 Assess and plan the change

10870.sentence: Those undertaking the assessment should make a recommendation on what course of action should be taken and why.
10870.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10870.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.5 Assess and plan the change

10870.sentence: Once the assessment and plan are ready for a decision, the change control register should be updated.
10870.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10870.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.5 Assess and plan the change

10871.sentence: After assessing a change request, a decision should be made on whether to approve, reject or defer the change.
10871.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10871.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.6 Decide on the change

10871.sentence: The decision should be backed by the impact assessment, supported by evidence where possible, including possible implementation options and taking account of the associated risks.
10871.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10871.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.6 Decide on the change

10871.sentence: If inability to make the change threatens the viability of the work overall, then this should be escalated through governance such as to the portfolio director or senior responsible owner.
10871.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10871.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.6 Decide on the change

10871.sentence: The change control register should be updated with the status and the change control manager, change owner, relevant team members and stakeholders notified.
10871.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10871.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.6 Decide on the change

10872.sentence: If a proposed change is approved, the change should be implemented in accordance with the plan, and the change control register updated.
10872.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10872.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.7 Implement, monitor and report on the change

10872.sentence: Relevant configuration items such as baselines, documentation, and deliverables should be updated (see Chapter 23: Traceability management).
10872.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10872.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.7 Implement, monitor and report on the change

10872.sentence: Actions taken to implement the change should be monitored and reported to ensure that the change is being carried out effectively, and those who need to know about the change and its progress in implementation are informed, such as impacted team managers and stakeholders.
10872.actor: Actions taken to implement the change
10872.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10872.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.7 Implement, monitor and report on the change

10872.sentence: The change control register should be updated regularly to reflect the current understanding of the change as well as its impact and implementation.
10872.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10872.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.7 Implement, monitor and report on the change

10873.sentence: A change request should be closed once the change has been confirmed as being implemented or rejected.
10873.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10873.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.8 Close the change request

10873.sentence: The change control register should be updated.
10873.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10873.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.8 Close the change request

10873.sentence: Closed changes should be kept on the register.
10873.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10873.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.8 Close the change request

10873.sentence: The registry entry should record when and by who the change was closed, as this information can be useful for identifying likely sources of risks when conducting lessons learned reviews (see Chapter 38: Learning from experience ) and for maintaining traceability (see Chapter 23: Traceability management).
10873.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10873.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.8 Close the change request

10874.sentence: Once the work has been completed and change control is no longer needed, the change control manager should close the management framework, retaining information and data in accordance with the delivery and sponsoring body’s information retention policy (see Chapter 24: Information and data management).
10874.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10874.headingPath: Chapter 22: Change control > 22.6 How to control change > 22.6.3 Key activities in controlling change > 22.6.3.9 Close the change control management framework

10878.sentence: changing elements that should be locked
10878.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10878.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.3 Why manage traceability?

10880.sentence: There should be two-way traceability from the higher-level to the lower-level components and back that comprise a solution as well as among different components.
10880.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10880.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.4 What is traceability management? > 23.4.2 How traceability connects the solution with management documentation

10882.sentence: If not done properly, there would be no evidential basis for decision-making and the programme or project should be considered out of control.
10882.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10882.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.5 Who manages traceability?

10882.sentence: Once in use the respective versions, statuses, relationships and baselines should be maintained until disposed of.
10882.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10882.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.5 Who manages traceability?

10882.sentence: If the solution or part of it is being undertaken by a supplier, the respective contract should state the obligations regarding traceability and include the amount of information the supplier is required to disclose and the rights of the sponsoring organisation to review or audit the work and records.
10882.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10882.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.5 Who manages traceability?

10883.sentence: Traceability is closely related to change control and information and data management and should be managed together, as shown in Figure 23.3.
10883.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10883.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.6 How to manage traceability > 23.6.1 What to consider when managing traceability > 23.6.1.1 Managing traceability, change control and information and data

10883.sentence: Figure 23.3 Traceability, change control and information and data management should be managed together
10883.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10883.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.6 How to manage traceability > 23.6.1 What to consider when managing traceability > 23.6.1.1 Managing traceability, change control and information and data

10883.sentence: Those working on or responsible for a solution should be confident they are working with the right versions of documentation and interfacing with the correct versions of the solution’s parts.
10883.actor: Those working on or responsible for a solution
10883.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10883.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.6 How to manage traceability > 23.6.1 What to consider when managing traceability > 23.6.1.1 Managing traceability, change control and information and data

10884.sentence: For example, a change to a plan should not be approved if it no longer fits within the constraints of the approved business case.
10884.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10884.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.6 How to manage traceability > 23.6.1 What to consider when managing traceability > 23.6.1.2 Defining the baselines

10884.sentence: In a programme and project, a baseline with an appropriate horizon should be set as soon as work to initiate has been completed.
10884.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10884.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.6 How to manage traceability > 23.6.1 What to consider when managing traceability > 23.6.1.2 Defining the baselines

10885.sentence: The scope and timing of these reviews should be coordinated to inform the formal assurance reviews and decision points (also known as gates), before starting a new phase of work (see Chapter 4: Governance and management).
10885.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10885.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.6 How to manage traceability > 23.6.1 What to consider when managing traceability > 23.6.1.3 Planning reviews of the solution

10887.sentence: Preparation for traceability management should start as part of initiating the portfolio, programme or project.
10887.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10887.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.6 How to manage traceability > 23.6.2 Preparing to manage traceability > 23.6.2.1 Choose which deliverables need to be traceable and how they are structured

10887.sentence: Each output, product, deliverable that requires approval is often called a traceability or configuration item and should be uniquely identified with its version and status.
10887.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10887.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.6 How to manage traceability > 23.6.2 Preparing to manage traceability > 23.6.2.1 Choose which deliverables need to be traceable and how they are structured

10887.sentence: As each output, product or deliverable is verified, successful completion should represent a milestone on the schedule, thereby tying the plan to each deliverable.
10887.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10887.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.6 How to manage traceability > 23.6.2 Preparing to manage traceability > 23.6.2.1 Choose which deliverables need to be traceable and how they are structured

10887.sentence: The outputs, products and deliverables should also be traceable and verifiable items within the traceability management framework.
10887.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10887.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.6 How to manage traceability > 23.6.2 Preparing to manage traceability > 23.6.2.1 Choose which deliverables need to be traceable and how they are structured

10890.sentence: The approach to managing traceability should be defined, including any processes, methods, tools and techniques to be used.
10890.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10890.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.6 How to manage traceability > 23.6.3 Key activities in managing traceability > 23.6.3.2 Develop and maintain the traceability management framework

10890.sentence: The management framework should be monitored to make sure it remains effective and appropriate as the work proceeds and address relevant feedback from its use.
10890.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10890.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.6 How to manage traceability > 23.6.3 Key activities in managing traceability > 23.6.3.2 Develop and maintain the traceability management framework

10891.sentence: The components of the plan, solution design and management documentation which need to be traced should be identified and the links defined.
10891.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10891.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.6 How to manage traceability > 23.6.3 Key activities in managing traceability > 23.6.3.3 Identify items to be traced

10891.sentence: If models and interim solutions are needed, these should also be included.
10891.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10891.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.6 How to manage traceability > 23.6.3 Key activities in managing traceability > 23.6.3.3 Identify items to be traced

10891.sentence: Each item should have a unique identifier, with two-way traceability running both ways between higher and lower levels of the hierarchy and across the elements at the same level.
10891.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10891.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.6 How to manage traceability > 23.6.3 Key activities in managing traceability > 23.6.3.3 Identify items to be traced

10892.sentence: Baselines should be defined which represent a specific point in time and show achievement through the solution’s life cycle.
10892.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10892.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.6 How to manage traceability > 23.6.3 Key activities in managing traceability > 23.6.3.4 Define the traceability baselines needed

10892.sentence: Each baseline should include the traceability items that comprise it and the two-way relationships among them.
10892.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10892.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.6 How to manage traceability > 23.6.3 Key activities in managing traceability > 23.6.3.4 Define the traceability baselines needed

10893.sentence: When formal changes to items are approved, the relevant version, status and relationships should be updated.
10893.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10893.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.6 How to manage traceability > 23.6.3 Key activities in managing traceability > 23.6.3.5 Control traceable items

10894.sentence: The status of each baseline and its constituent items, and its relationship to other items, should be available to those who need them to undertake their work.
10894.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10894.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.6 How to manage traceability > 23.6.3 Key activities in managing traceability > 23.6.3.6 Report traceability status

10896.sentence: Once the solution has been fully disposed of, the information should be archived in accordance with the sponsoring organisation’s information retention policy (see Chapter 24: Information and data management) and the management framework closed.
10896.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10896.headingPath: Chapter 23: Traceability management > 23.6 How to manage traceability > 23.6.3 Key activities in managing traceability > 23.6.3.8 Close the traceability management framework

candidateConflicts.sourceTitle: The Digital, Data and Technology Playbook
candidateConflicts.sentence: If required for a reprocurement, then data and information must be transferred to the contracting authority in time for it to be given to upcoming bidders.

10898.sentence: Information and data should be managed in line with the government’s principles on transparency, accountability and fairness.
10898.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10898.headingPath: Chapter 24: Information and data management > 24.2 Key points

10898.sourceTitle: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government
10898.headingPath: Chapter 24: Information and data management > 24.2 Key points

10898.sentence: Information and data relating to the design and development of the solution should be transferred to the in-life owner for future management and use.

10898.headingPath: Chapter 24: Information and data management > 24.2 Key points

10901.sentence: Pre-existing data and information should already have an assigned information owner who should be consulted on its use and handling.

10901.headingPath: Chapter 24: Information and data management > 24.5 Who is responsible for information and data management?
